newsitem.title: UK: Base metal rally stirs memories of 1993/94.
newsitem.headline: Base metal rally stirs memories of 1993/94.

text.p: Latest gains in London Metal Exchange (LME) non-ferrous metals prices, boosted by investment fund interest, have led some analysts to suggest that they may signal another bull run in the sector.
On Thursday, zinc climbed to its best for nearly two years. Aluminium hit an eight-month peak, tin and nickel rose to their best for four months and lead touched two-month highs.
And 1997 has also seen major investment houses issuing metal basket warrants and notes - not seen since the last bull market.
"It could be the return of 1993/94 when they were last issued," said William Adams of LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co.
Earlier this week Goldman Sachs International issued warrants on a basket of metals, as well as call warrants on copper, zinc, aluminium and its commodity index.
On Thursday, Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) launched a $100 million issue linked to the value of aluminium, copper, platinum and crude oil.
Traders said these instruments, which have a bias towards calls and could well be followed by others in coming weeks, were positive for the metals market.
"I do seem to remember that there were a whole host of them a couple of years ago - they seemed to snowball as well," one trader said.
"We get bullish when we see this, as the metal is going into strong hands," another added.
He said that the institutions involved in that niche of the market would typically have buyers lined up for the issues, and would already have their hedge cover in place.
This influx of investment fund money has implications for longer-term metal price movements as well, analysts said.
"Consumers have not forgotten how they got caught in 1994," said Nick Moore of the Flemings Global Mining Group.
"If 1997 is to be a re-run of 1994 then they would be unwise to twiddle their thumbs waiting for lower prices. The time for bottom fishing has passed," he added.
Wolff's Adams noted that in the previous bull-run, the investment-fund rally lifted prices at a time when metal inventories were rising and were at much higher levels.
"There is much more potential now, as stock levels are lower if they (funds) come in," he said.
